items.title: Annuli in the complex plane
Convergent Laurent series on an annulus
The principal part of a Laurent series
Isolated singularities: removable, poles, and essential singularities
Simple poles
Meromorphic functions on a plane domain
Laurent expansion on an annulus
items.strategy: Use the outer-minus-inner circle cycle in the annulus, apply the global Cauchy formula there, and expand the Cauchy kernels geometrically on the inner and outer regions. The positive and negative powers then assemble into one locally uniformly convergent Laurent series on the annulus.

items.title: Laurent coefficients are given by contour integrals and are unique
items.strategy: Integrate the Laurent expansion term by term on any intermediate circle and use the circle integrals of integer powers to isolate each coefficient. Uniqueness follows because those coefficient integrals are determined by the function, so two Laurent expansions on the same annulus must agree term by term.

items.title: Laurent coefficients are independent of the intermediate radius
items.strategy: Compare the coefficient integrals on two circles inside the same annulus. The difference is the integral over the annular two-circle cycle, which vanishes by the global Cauchy theorem.

items.title: The residue of an isolated singularity
Laurent series split into regular and principal parts
items.strategy: Split the Laurent series into its nonnegative and negative powers, show that each subseries converges on its natural domain, and use coefficient uniqueness to prove that the resulting decomposition is unique.

items.title: Characterizations of removable singularities
items.strategy: Expand the punctured-disc function into a Laurent series and show that boundedness near the center forces the principal part to vanish. The extension, boundedness, and limit conditions are then matched one by one to the absence of negative coefficients.

items.title: Characterizations of poles
items.strategy: Compare the finite principal part with the reciprocal of the holomorphic factor. A finite nonzero principal part gives growth like |z-a|^{-m}; conversely, if |f(z)| tends to infinity then 1/f is bounded and has a removable zero whose order recovers the pole order.

items.title: Every isolated singularity is removable, a pole, or essential
items.strategy: Use the regular-principal decomposition to separate the three Laurent-series possibilities: no negative coefficients, finitely many negative coefficients, or infinitely many negative coefficients. The removable and pole characterizations identify the first two cases, and the remaining case is essential.

items.title: Casorati-Weierstrass theorem
items.strategy: Argue contrapositively. If the image of a punctured neighbourhood misses an open disc about some value w, then 1/(f-w) is bounded there, so the removable-singularity theorem extends it holomorphically; this forces f-w to be removable or a pole, contradicting essentiality.

items.title: The residue is the normalized small-circle integral
items.strategy: Apply the Laurent coefficient formula at n = -1. The residue is exactly the coefficient isolated by the normalized contour integral.

items.title: At a simple pole the residue is the limit of (z-a)f(z)
items.strategy: Write the function as g(z)/(z-a) with g holomorphic and nonzero at a. The Laurent coefficient of (z-a)^{-1} is then g(a), which is also the displayed limit by continuity.

items.title: Residue formula for a pole of order m
items.strategy: Write f(z)=g(z)/(z-a)^m with g holomorphic at a. The residue is the coefficient of (z-a)^{m-1} in the Taylor series of g, which the higher-derivative Cauchy formula identifies with g^{(m-1)}(a)/(m-1)!.

items.title: Residues of p over q at a simple zero of q
items.strategy: Extend q(z)/(z-a) holomorphically across a by the difference quotient, note that its value at a is q'(a), and rewrite p/q as a simple pole with holomorphic numerator p divided by that extension.

items.title: Isolated singularities at infinity
Poles of a meromorphic function form a closed discrete set and are at most countable
items.strategy: Each pole is isolated by definition, so the pole set is discrete. A limit point inside the domain would contradict isolatedness, hence the pole set is closed in the domain. Countability follows by intersecting the discrete set with a countable compact exhaustion, or equivalently by assigning to each pole a rational disc meeting no other pole.

title: Isolated Singularities and Laurent Series — Examples

items.title: The same rational function has different Laurent series on different annuli
items.strategy: Expand 1/(z(z-1)) by geometric series in the regions 0<|z|<1 and 1<|z|<∞, and also expand it about z=1. The example is there to make the annulus dependence of Laurent expansions explicit rather than implicit.

items.title: Polynomials have poles at infinity and reciprocal polynomials have removable singularities there
items.strategy: For f(z)=z^m, rewrite f(1/w)=w^{-m}; for f(z)=1/z^m, rewrite f(1/w)=w^m. The translated classifications at w=0 are exactly the definitions at infinity.

items.title: The residue of e^z/z^3 from the pole-derivative formula
items.strategy: Treat e^z/z^3 as a pole of order three at 0 and apply the derivative formula to the holomorphic factor e^z. The second derivative of e^z at 0 is still 1, so the residue is immediate once the factorial is in place.

items.title: A residue of p over q at a simple zero is p(a)/q'(a)
items.strategy: Pick a concrete quotient with a simple denominator zero and evaluate the residue with the quotient formula. Then differentiate the denominator once at the zero to show the shortcut matches the local-factor computation.

items.title: Zero residue does not imply a removable singularity
items.strategy: Use 1/z^2 at 0. Its Laurent coefficient of (z-a)^{-1} is 0, but the singularity is a pole of order two, so residue zero is weaker than removability.

items.title: e^{1/z} has an essential singularity at 0 and omits the value 0
items.strategy: Its Laurent series has infinitely many negative powers, so the singularity is essential. The exponential never vanishes, so this one omitted value shows why Casorati-Weierstrass gives density rather than surjectivity.

items.title: sin(1/z) has an essential singularity at 0
items.strategy: Expand complex sine through its exponential definition and substitute 1/z. The resulting Laurent series has infinitely many negative powers, so the singularity is essential.

items.title: 1/sin(1/z) has a nonisolated singularity at 0
items.strategy: The real zeros nπ of sine produce poles at z=1/(nπ), which accumulate at 0. So the point 0 is a singularity of the function, but not an isolated one.

items.title: A Laurent series on a punctured disc can have infinitely many negative powers
items.strategy: Use sin(1/z) or e^{1/z} as the witness. The point is not the particular coefficients, but the failure of the 'finite principal part' expectation outside the pole case.

title: Harmonic Functions and the Poisson Integral

items.title: Plane harmonic functions
Agreement with the earlier C^2 holomorphic-components theorem
items.strategy: Record that the published C^2 holomorphic-components theorem proves the same Laplace-equation conclusion starting from a holomorphic function. This page keeps that convention and develops the converse direction from harmonic data.

items.title: Every plane harmonic function is locally the real part of a holomorphic function
items.strategy: For harmonic u, the combination u_x-iu_y satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations by the mixed-partial theorem, hence is holomorphic. On a small disc it has a primitive, and the real part of that primitive has the same first partials as u, so the two differ by a constant.

items.title: Harmonic conjugates
Harmonic conjugates exist on homologically simply connected plane domains
items.strategy: Apply the local construction globally to g=u_x-iu_y. On a homologically simply connected domain g has a primitive G; the real part of G has the same gradient as u, so u-Re(G) is constant and the imaginary part of G is the desired harmonic conjugate.

items.title: Two harmonic conjugates differ by a real constant
items.strategy: If u+iv_1 and u+iv_2 are holomorphic, then i(v_1-v_2) is holomorphic and real-valued. A real-valued holomorphic function on a domain is constant, so v_1-v_2 is constant as well.

items.title: Plane harmonic functions are smooth and real analytic
items.strategy: Near each point, a harmonic function is the real part of a holomorphic function. The published analyticity theorem for holomorphic functions then transfers smoothness and real analyticity to the harmonic function.

items.title: The circle and disc mean-value properties
Plane harmonic functions satisfy the mean-value property
items.strategy: Write the harmonic function locally as the real part of a holomorphic function. Apply the holomorphic mean-value property to that holomorphic potential, then integrate the circle averages radially to obtain the disc average formula.

items.title: Maximum and minimum principles for plane harmonic functions
items.strategy: On a disc, represent the harmonic function as the real part of a holomorphic function and apply the maximum principle for real parts. The bounded-domain boundary form follows by applying the local statement to u and to -u.

items.title: The bounded plane Dirichlet problem has at most one continuous harmonic solution
items.strategy: Take the difference of two harmonic solutions with the same boundary data and apply the maximum and minimum principles to the difference.

items.title: A plane harmonic function bounded above or below is constant
items.strategy: On the plane, choose a global harmonic conjugate and form an entire holomorphic potential F. If the harmonic function is bounded above, then exp(F) is bounded entire; if it is bounded below, then exp(-F) is. Liouville then makes F constant.

items.title: A plane harmonic function that vanishes on a nonempty open set vanishes everywhere on the domain
items.strategy: Let S be the union of open subsets on which u vanishes. It is open by definition. If a point lies in the closure of S, a local holomorphic potential has real part zero on a nonempty open subset of a disc, so the maximum principle for real parts forces that potential to be constant on the disc; hence the point lies in S. Thus S is nonempty, open, and closed in the connected domain.

items.title: Plane harmonicity is preserved by holomorphic and antiholomorphic changes of coordinate
items.strategy: For a holomorphic change of variable, precompose a local holomorphic potential with the map and take real parts. For an antiholomorphic change of variable, compose once more with complex conjugation to reduce to the holomorphic case.

items.title: The Poisson kernel on the unit disc
The Poisson kernel is positive, has total mass one, and concentrates at a boundary point
items.strategy: Positivity is immediate from the formula. The unit-mass statement comes from the corresponding holomorphic circle average, and the concentration estimate is proved by bounding the kernel uniformly on the complement of a short arc.

items.title: The Poisson integral on the unit disc
Poisson integrals are harmonic on the unit disc
items.strategy: Differentiate under the integral sign with respect to the real coordinates on compactly smaller discs. The explicit kernel satisfies Laplace's equation in the disc variable, so its convolution with continuous boundary data is harmonic.

items.title: The Poisson kernel is a boundary approximate identity
items.strategy: Split the boundary integral into a short arc around the target point and its complement. Continuity of the datum controls the nearby arc, while the concentration estimate from the kernel-properties lemma drives the far arc to zero uniformly.

items.title: The Poisson integral gives the unique continuous harmonic extension on the closed unit disc
items.strategy: Combine harmonicity of Poisson integrals with the boundary approximate-identity lemma to get existence, and use the maximum/minimum principle on the difference of two candidates for uniqueness.

items.title: A harmonic function is recovered from its values on any containing circle by the Poisson formula
items.strategy: Fix a smaller concentric disc, apply the Poisson integral theorem to the boundary values of the harmonic function on the larger circle, and identify the resulting extension with the given function by Dirichlet uniqueness.

items.title: A continuous plane function with the local mean-value property is harmonic
items.strategy: On a compactly contained disc, solve the Dirichlet problem for the boundary values of u by the Poisson integral. The difference between that harmonic solution and u still has the local mean-value property and vanishes on the boundary, so the mean-value maximum principle forces the difference to vanish.

items.title: A bounded harmonic function near an isolated puncture extends harmonically
items.strategy: On the punctured disc, the complex gradient u_x-iu_y is holomorphic. Local boundedness of u and a local harmonic conjugate on small circles give the estimate |u_x-iu_y|<=C/|z-a|, so (z-a)(u_x-iu_y) is bounded and the removable-singularity theorem extends it holomorphically across the puncture. The remaining residue obstruction vanishes, so the extended derivative has a primitive whose real part differs from u by a constant, giving the harmonic extension.

items.title: Positive harmonic functions on a disc satisfy Harnack's inequality
items.strategy: Represent the function by the Poisson formula on a containing circle and compare the Poisson kernel at two interior points by its explicit extremal bounds. The resulting ratio estimate is the Harnack inequality.

items.title: An increasing harmonic sequence converges locally uniformly to a harmonic limit or diverges to +infinity
items.strategy: Either the sequence diverges to +infinity at every point, or it is bounded at one point and Harnack's inequality makes it locally uniformly bounded on smaller discs. Poisson representation on those discs then turns monotone pointwise convergence into local uniform convergence to a harmonic limit.

items.title: Harmonic and holomorphic Schwarz reflection across the real axis
items.strategy: For the harmonic statement on an upper half-disc, reflect the boundary values oddly on the circle and compare the Poisson solution with the given function by Dirichlet uniqueness. For the holomorphic statement, apply harmonic reflection to the imaginary part and recover the reflected holomorphic function by the harmonic-conjugate construction; the explicit lower-half formula is F(z)=overline{f(conj z)}.

title: Harmonic Functions and the Poisson Integral — Examples

items.title: log|z| is harmonic on the punctured plane
items.strategy: Write log|z| as (1/2)log(x^2+y^2) and differentiate twice directly on C\{0}. The Laplacian cancels exactly, so this standard witness really is harmonic away from the origin.

items.title: The real parts of z^n are harmonic polynomials
items.strategy: The polynomial z^n is entire, so its real part is harmonic by the earlier holomorphic-components theorem. Expand a few low-degree cases explicitly to connect the abstract statement with concrete harmonic polynomials.

items.title: 2xy is a harmonic conjugate of x^2-y^2
items.strategy: Use z^2=(x^2-y^2)+2ixy. The example is the fastest concrete instance of the local-potential theorem and gives an explicit conjugate pair to cite later.

items.title: The Poisson integral of cos(theta) is r cos(theta)
items.strategy: Insert the boundary datum cos(theta) into the Poisson integral and identify the resulting function with the harmonic real part of z by uniqueness of the disc Dirichlet problem.

items.title: The Poisson kernel realizes the sharp Harnack bounds on concentric discs
items.strategy: Evaluate the Poisson kernel at the extremal boundary angle and compare its values at the center and an interior radial point. The computation shows exactly where the disc Harnack constants come from.

items.title: log|z| has no global harmonic conjugate on C\{0}
items.strategy: If log|z| had a harmonic conjugate v on C\{0}, then log|z|+iv would be a continuous logarithm of the identity function on the punctured plane. The published no-continuous-logarithm theorem rules that out.

items.title: A harmonic function can vanish on a line without being zero everywhere
items.strategy: Take u(x,y)=x. It is harmonic on the whole plane, vanishes on the y-axis, and is not the zero function, so vanishing on a curve is weaker than vanishing on a nonempty open set.

items.title: The product of two harmonic functions need not be harmonic
items.strategy: Take u(x,y)=x and v(x,y)=x. Each is harmonic, but uv=x^2 has Laplacian 2, so the product leaves the harmonic class.

items.title: Re(1/z) is harmonic on a punctured disc and does not extend harmonically across 0
items.strategy: The rational function 1/z is holomorphic on the punctured disc, so its real part is harmonic there. Its values are unbounded near 0 along the real axis, so the bounded removable-singularity theorem does not apply and no harmonic extension across 0 exists.
